tagline: County-line signs name the musicians along a four-lane road through eastern Kentucky.
intro: The Country Music Highway follows US 23 through eastern Kentucky on four lanes, with additional lanes in some cities. The road parallels the Ohio and Big Sandy rivers in the north and passes through Pikeville’s mountain cut farther south. The Federal Highway Administration lists this National Scenic Byway as 144.1 miles, allowing two to three driving hours, and describes a heritage route linking music, coal mining, crafts and architecture.

US 23 entered Kentucky in 1929, initially ending at Pikeville. Later, as Appalachian coal employment declined, workers took the highway north toward industrial cities. In 1994, a bill sponsored by State Representative Hubert Collins gave Kentucky’s route its Country Music Highway name to recognize musicians from the counties it crossed. Loretta Lynn, Crystal Gayle, Hylo Brown and Dwight Yoakam are among the performers noted along the Kentucky highway. County-line signs list those performers, and the museum in Paintsville extends that tribute.

Head south from Greenup along the Ohio toward Ashland and Catlettsburg, then follow the Big Sandy valley toward Louisa. Continue to Paintsville, with Butcher Hollow in the Van Lear community as a separate excursion. US 23 bypasses Paintsville and Prestonsburg before reaching the Pikeville Cut-Through. Beyond Pikeville, the road continues toward Jenkins and the Virginia line.
notice: At county lines, signs list country music performers from that county.

moments.title: Paintsville
moments.text: Paintsville’s U.S. 23 Country Music Highway Museum profiles singers who grew up near the road, including Loretta Lynn, Crystal Gayle and Hylo Brown. Its subject extends beyond Paintsville to entertainers from across eastern Kentucky. Gayle was born in Paintsville in 1951; her older sister Lynn was born in nearby Butcher Hollow. The museum opened in the early 2000s, after the highway received its musical name. The town occupies bottomland where Paint Creek meets the Levisa Fork, amid the Appalachian foothills. US 23 serves as its bypass, while South Mayo Trail is the main business route.

moments.title: Butcher Hollow
moments.text: Loretta Lynn’s birthplace belongs to the Van Lear coal community, although Butcher Hollow is often listed as a separate town. Her song “Coal Miner’s Daughter” names both Butcher Hollow and the Van Lear mines. Consolidation Coal Company built Van Lear in the early twentieth century. Five mines operated there from 1910 through 1946. When the company divested its local properties, residents of company houses received the first chance to buy their homes, and many did. Butcher Hollow has used a Van Lear mailing address since the post office opened in 1909.

moments.title: Pikeville Cut-Through
moments.text: A road, railroad and river share the cut through Peach Orchard Mountain. The opening is 523 feet deep, completed in 1987 after fourteen years of work by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. The cut measures 1,300 feet across and extends for 3,700 feet. Mayor William Hambley first proposed moving the railroad to reduce coal dust from trains passing through town. The plan expanded to include the highway and a new course for the Levisa Fork to address repeated flooding. Workers filled the former riverbed to create land for development. Hambley Boulevard occupies the old railbed.
